summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the measurement (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 4 wholes hold 20. The central challenge is that the quotient is BIGGER than the dividend, which collides with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a length model, using prediction then counting, estimation to police reasonableness, and the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.
misconceptions: Quotient must be smaller than the dividend, so 4 ÷ 1/5 'can't' be 20 (whole-number over-generalisation that division shrinks)
Divides by the denominator instead: 4 ÷ 1/5 read as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (treats the unit fraction as its denominator)
Confuses with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 (imports the more-familiar operation)
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers rather than 1/5 as one quantity

activities.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar
steps: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
activities.insight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.

activities.title: Estimate first to catch absurd answers
steps: Before computing, estimate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the dividend, and roughly how big.
Work an example like 5 ÷ 5/6: reason that because 5/6 is nearly 1 whole, the answer is a little more than 5.
Check a worked answer for reasonableness: decide whether 0.8 could possibly be the answer to 4 ÷ 1/5, and explain why not.
State a rule of thumb: dividing by a piece smaller than 1 gives more copies than the number of wholes.
activities.insight: Estimation acts as a reasonableness check: an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is immediately caught as absurd because many small fifths must fit in 4 wholes.

activities.title: Prove it with the inverse multiplication
steps: After counting 20 fifths in 4 wholes, write the matching multiplication: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
Explain in words how the multiplication just learned justifies the division answer.
Gather or redraw the 20 fifths into 4 wholes to show the multiplication rebuilding the original dividend.
Apply the same check to a fresh case, e.g. verify 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 by showing 24 × 1/4 = 6.
activities.insight: Division by a unit fraction and the related multiplication are inverse statements about the same quantity, so the multiplication check confirms the division.

activities.title: Invent and solve a measurement story
steps: Invent a real context for a whole ÷ unit-fraction, e.g. 'how many 1/4-cup scoops are in 6 cups?' or 'how many 1/3-cup scoops in this jug?'
Before counting, predict out loud whether there will be more or fewer scoops than the number of whole cups, and say why.
Solve the story by counting the pieces and state the answer with its meaning.
Match several division expressions (e.g. 6 ÷ 1/4, 4 ÷ 1/5) to the correct 'how many … in …' story.
activities.insight: Owning the measurement structure through a self-made context makes the 'how many fit' meaning transferable rather than memorised.

activities.title: Check your understanding (prediction, count, and reasoning)
steps: Answer 'how many 1/5 fit in 4?' using a number-line count or slider, giving 20.

Answer a multiple-choice item for 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24, ruling out derivable distractors such as 1.5 (from the denominator-division error 6 ÷ 4) and a value smaller than the dividend (from the 'division shrinks' misconception).
Order several whole ÷ unit-fraction quotients by size to expose the 'answer must be smaller' misconception.
For any answer, add a sentence saying WHY it is bigger than the dividend; a correct number without a correct reason is incomplete.
activities.insight: A genuine grasp of the measurement meaning produces both the right quotient AND a 'how many fit' justification; recalling a number alone is not sufficient.

checkQuestion: Work out 4 ÷ 1/5. Then tell me why the answer comes out that way — is it bigger or smaller than 4, and how would you explain that to someone who thinks dividing always makes a number smaller?
checkAnswer: 20. Because 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit in 4 wholes?' — each whole contains 5 fifths, and 4 wholes contain 4 × 5 = 20. It is BIGGER than 4 because the pieces are small, so many of them fit; check: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
